en: While my falcon head remains,
There is no one who can equal me.
My argali lies upon my mountain pass,
My duck lies upon my lake.
My fox lies, Karagul,
Where I placed it in safekeeping.
Great Beijing is a wondrous city—
I traveled to its farthest edge;
All Beijing is an ancient city—
I traveled to its very foundation.
Giving Algara no rest,
I, a renowned great noble,
Came roaming back from the Kakan.
No pass remains that I have not crossed,
No land remains that I have not trodden;
Crossing passes and treading stones,
Algara grew lean,
His manifest blood thickened,
And Algara grew old.
I traveled through many lands;
There is no gray, ridged mountain left,
And no enemy left to face me.
No foe remains for me to grapple with;
I will turn Algara loose—
Let him grow stout, with no regret.
In winter, take the horses
Up to Kyr-Kayyn to winter.
For every horse herder,
Have marmot fur sewn upon his shoulders.
When autumn comes,
Graze them in autumn at gray Kürpüldök;
When spring comes,
Drive them along the Sary-Suu!
Great Lord Khan Kongurbai—
Have you heard,
Worthy lord, of the deeds I have done?
My brow is high and my venom strong;
While my splendid life remains,
I will straighten out anyone who challenges me!
Will anyone approach and escape me?
Will one who meets me pass without dying?
Beneath me is Algara;
I possess my courser Algara—
Will one who fights me remain alive?
While my splendid life remains,
Will anyone come swarming against me?
Will a man grapple with me and win?
Will any doomed man come before me?
Will he bend me and take me captive?
Will one who wrestles with me remain alive?
My saddlecloth is made of leather;
Known throughout this world
Is my valor, Kongurbai’s valor!
Yesterday—have you heard?
When chaos broke loose,
When the Bloodthirsty One came
And wrested away the khanate of Beijing,
When his undertaking reached Beijing,
Untouched even by Alexander,
When he took countless riches and girls
As plunder,
When he ravaged the throne,
And slaughtered many heroes,
Dust rose from his advance
And souls fled at the sound of him.
In his fury, Khan Manas
Drained the people of the Kakan;
That Bloodthirsty One whose home burned
At last died by my own hand.
Infidel and Muslim
Stood their ground and fought,
When hero Kozhozhash, the great marksman,
Performed immeasurable feats of valor,
When Almambet and Chubak,
Baichoro and Syrgak,
Were all slaughtered in succession,
When Akkula fell to a bullet,
And yesterday, when Almambet died a martyr,
The blood-drinking Bloodthirsty One
Lifted his saddle and tack
And was left on foot in the field.
The lion’s courage at the edge of death—
The courage of that desperate
Burut doomed to die—
Was shown then.
His rage began in earnest;
Beginning with Kozhozhash,
He shot down eight
Of the treasury marksmen.
Gathering courage and making ready,
Six thousand Chinese and countless kaldais
Drew bows like pouring rain
And shot arrows like hail;
With my splendid self at their head,
We made ready and closed in to seize him.
Then powder spilled from his powder flask;
He despaired of his grieving life,
Stepped ponderously and braced himself,
Leaned upon Akkelte,
And that Bloodthirsty One stood there.
Before one could say this or that,
In the blink of an eye,
Riding a horse like a blue courser,
Wearing a blue lynx-fur cap,
His gray-wolf companion Bakai,
The Bloodthirsty One’s true confidant,
Opened the great slaughter.
Before one could say this or that,
In the blink of an eye,
He put the six thousand Chinese and countless kaldais
All to the sword and slaughtered them.
He revealed his might;
Then mighty Bakai
Mounted the champion Manas,
The Bloodthirsty One, upon Arbuurul.
His eyes blazed like fire;
The bloodlust truly seized
The accursed Burut,
And his rage began in earnest.
He utterly slaughtered
The Chinese as numerous as stones.
In the battle that day,
The mighty men in armor died,
And the stone-countless host was wiped out.
He mounted Taibuurul
And drove the teeming Chinese
As far as the Kakan.
His rage began in earnest;
Of the tightly barred gates,
He smashed five at once
And demolished them completely.
When the Bloodthirsty One withdrew,
I reconnoitered the road behind him;
I deliberately stayed and stalked him.
Azhybai, whom he posted as lookout,
Had fallen into a deep sleep;
I went straight toward him
And struck the thick shaft
Hard against solid bone as I passed.
My spear reached him,
And he went away wounded.
Concealing his wound without speaking,
The Bloodthirsty One let it fester and died, they say.
His own kin turned hostile,
And divided his possessions
In the hands of the orphaned child, they say.
That bitch Kanykei of old
Carried him away along the border,
And scattered much of her wealth, they say.
Carrying her child upon her back,
She fled toward Karakhan, they say.
Into the city of Khan Temir
She wandered and disappeared, they say;
Into the city of Karakhan
She fled and disappeared, they say.
Thus bereaved Kanykei departed,
And Semetey fled away.
Living as an orphan, he grew to manhood,
Joined the people of the land,
Grew broad and vigorous, and became a hero,
The equal of any hero’s son.
He came and settled in Talas, they say,
And became manifestly a gray wolf
Far surpassing his father, they say.
I heard he settled in Talas,
At shrub-filled Keng-Kol.
I heard the Bloodthirsty One’s son Semetey
Sucked dry
Whoever offered resistance.
He emerged a greater hero than his father,
A lion who convulsed the world;
His name is heard scorching the earth.
I received it from the transmitters of tradition
And asked those who knew.
I heard that orphan did as he pleased
To every one
Who challenged him.
I heard he cut down
Anyone who crossed his path.
I fear that accursed one,
For they say that orphan is coming;
They say he will gird his waist firmly
And pursue Manas’s blood-price
From us who dwell in Beijing.
They say the misbegotten son is coming,
Gathering troops and assembling an army.
They say he will bring distress upon Beijing.
Whether alive or dead,
That splendid man and I
Will face one another, they say.
I hear reports from messengers;
I hear that champion, son of the Bloodthirsty One,
Will not refrain from challenging us.
They say he is a valiant man who will clash;
If his strength suffices, they say,
He will battle even the Kakan.
I heard he surpasses
His father Manas, the gray wolf.
I heard he does whatever he pleases
In the land where he rules.
When his wrath was roused,
I heard he slaughtered them all,
Beginning with his own father, Khan Zhakyp.
With no soul left to protest,
I heard a hero had arisen—
An infidel fiercer
Than Manas, I heard.
He is no son who will stand and watch,
No slave who will refrain from grappling.
You were a hero, Karagul;
Be wary of this side!
When we fought in those days,
There was one called Bakai;
He was the finest man of all.
He was highly skilled among spearmen,
And was foremost at reading
The stratagems of the enemy.
He was a lion quick with a sword,
A hero who was a marksman with a gun.
Girded at his narrow waist,
He attacked Beijing alone,
That city too vast for the earth to bear.
His eyes blazed like a lion’s;
He regarded death as less than a hair
And carried Manas’s golden banner.
If a hero was speared, who speared him?
As I recall, hero Bakai speared him—
His fame remained beside Manas.
Wise and ingenious in stratagems,
Lion Bakai was a hero;
In wisdom and cunning
He was no less than Manas.
When he battled with us,
Bakai’s beard was mottled gray.
That Bakai must have died,
Must have beheld the face of Judgment Day.
If that Bakai has not died,
If he has not beheld the face of Judgment Day,
He would lead Semetey
And bring him here.
The reason he would bring him is this:
Was it not Bakai
Who brought chaos upon the Kakanchin?
Was it not Bakai
Who seized the khanate of Chet-Beijing?
Was it not Bakai who mounted
The golden throne where the khan sits?
Was it not Bakai
Who journeyed through Beijing on many campaigns?
The roads to Beijing have five branches—
Distinct as the five fingers of his hand—
Was it not Bakai who knew them?
Was it not Bakai who led campaigns
Against the Kakan and traveled
Through this land many times?
That Bakai will not disappear;
